akhfash:1-3.t:
﴿بِسْمِ اللهِ الرَّحْمٰنِ الرَّحِيـمِ﴾: "اسم" [in the basmala] is a redundant (zāʾida) connective, added so that by mentioning it the utterance leaves the domain of the oath and becomes an intention of seeking blessing, because the basic form of the speech is "بالله" (by Allah). The alif of "بسم" was dropped from the script as a lightening, because of frequent use, and because the bāʾ of attachment (bāʾ al-ilṣāq) makes it unnecessary in pronunciation and in writing. If you wrote "باسم الرحمن" or "باسم القادر" or "باسم القاهر", the alif would not be dropped.
The alif in "اسم" is a connecting alif (alif waṣl), because you say "سُمْيّ", and it was dropped because it is not part of the pronounced word.
(اب) [Translator's note: this marker appears thus in the source.] It is "اسمٌ", because when you form its diminutive you say "سُمَيّ", and the alif goes. And His words ﴿وَٱمْرَأَتُهُ حَمَّالَةَ ٱلْحَطَبِ﴾ and His words ﴿وَبَعَثْنَا مِنهُمُ ٱثْنَيْ عَشَرَ نَقِيباً﴾: this is a connecting alif, because you say "مُرَيَّة" and "ثُنَيَّا عشر". And [His words] ﴿فَٱنفَجَرَتْ مِنْهُ ٱثْنَتَا عَشْرَةَ عَيْناً﴾ is connecting, because you say "ثُنَيَّتا عشرةَ". He said ﴿إِذْ أَرْسَلْنَآ إِلَيْهِمُ ٱثْنَيْنِ فَكَذَّبُوهُمَا﴾, and He said ﴿مَا كَانَ أَبُوكِ ٱمْرَأَ سَوْءٍ﴾, because you say for "اثنين" "ثُنَيِّيّن" and for "آمرىء" "مُرَىّءِ", and the alif falls away. It was only added because of the sukūn (vowellessness) of the letter after it: when they wanted to begin with it, they could not start with a vowelless letter, so they introduced this alif in order to reach the speech by means of it. When [the speech] is joined to something before it, this alif is no longer needed. Likewise every alif at the start of a verb or a maṣdar (verbal noun), where the "يَفْعل" form of that verb has a fatḥa on its yāʾ, is a connecting alif, as in His words ﴿وَإِيَّاكَ نَسْتَعِينُ﴾ ﴿ٱهْدِنَا﴾, because you say "يَهْدِي" and the yāʾ has fatḥa. [Translator's note: the source cites ﴿وَإِيَّاكَ نَسْتَعِينُ﴾ before ﴿ٱهْدِنَا﴾ in this sequence; the example of a connecting alif is ﴿ٱهْدِنَا﴾.] And His words ﴿أُوْلَـٰئِكَ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱشْتَرُواْ ٱلضَّلاَلَةَ﴾, and [His words] ﴿يٰهَامَانُ ٱبْنِ لِي صَرْحاً﴾, and His words ﴿عَذَابٌ ٱرْكُضْ بِرِجْلِكَ﴾; there are many cases like this in the Quran. The reason in it is like the reason in "اسم" and "اثنين" and what resembles them: because the letter at the start of the verb was vowelless, they put this alif in it so as to reach the speech by it when they begin.
All these alifs (2ء) [Translator's note: this marker appears thus in the source.] that are in verbs have kasra when you begin with them. When you begin you say ﴿ٱهْدِنَا ٱلصّرَاطَ﴾, ﴿ٱبْنِ لِي﴾, ﴿ٱشْتَرُواْ ٱلضَّلاَلَةَ﴾ — except a verb whose third letter has ḍamma: then you give its first letter ḍamma when you begin, saying ﴿ٱرْكُضْ بِرِجْلِكَ﴾, and you say ﴿ٱذْكُرُواْ ٱللَّهَ كَثِيراً﴾. This alif was given ḍamma when the third letter has ḍamma only because they saw nothing between the two letters but one vowelless letter, and it was heavy for them to be in a kasra and then move to a ḍamma. So they wanted both to have ḍamma, since that does not change the meaning.
In some speech they said "مِنْتِن" for "المُنْتِن" (stinking). It comes only from "أنتن", so the participle is "مُنْتِن", like "أكرم", participle "مُكْرِم". They gave the mīm kasra because of the kasra of the tāʾ. And some gave the tāʾ ḍamma, saying "مُنْتُن", because of the ḍamma of the mīm. They also said "النِقِد" for "النَقِد", giving the nūn kasra because of the kasra of the qāf. This is not part of their speech except where the second letter is one of the six letters, as in "شعير". The six letters are: khāʾ, ḥāʾ, ʿayn, ghayn, hamza and hāʾ.
Whatever is on the pattern "فُعِلَ" (passive) among those beginning with this added alif is also begun with ḍamma, as in ﴿ٱجْتُثَّتْ مِن فَوْقِ ٱلأَرْضِ﴾, because the first letter of "فُعِلَ" always has ḍamma, and its third letter also has ḍamma.
Whatever is on the pattern "أَفعَلُ أنا" (I do) has a disjunctive alif (alif qaṭʿ), even if it is from a connecting-alif verb, because "أَفْعَلُ" contains an alif other than the connecting alif, and it is the counterpart of the yāʾ in "يَفْعَل". In the Book of Allah the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿ٱدْعُونِيۤ أَسْتَجِبْ لَكُمْ﴾, ﴿أَنَاْ آتِيكَ بِهِ﴾ and ﴿وَقَالَ ٱلْمَلِكُ ٱئْتُونِي بِهِ أَسْتَخْلِصْهُ لِنَفْسِي﴾.
Alifs of the kind that have no lām with them at the start of a noun and do not fall away in the diminutive are disjunctive; at the beginning they stay as they are in connection, as in His words ﴿هَذَآ أَخِي لَهُ تِسْعٌ﴾, His words ﴿يَٰأَبَانَآ﴾, His words ﴿إِنَّهَا لإِحْدَى ٱلْكُبَرِ﴾, ﴿قَالَتْ إِحْدَاهُمَا﴾ and ﴿حَتَّىٰ إِذَا جَآءَ أَحَدَهُمُ﴾, because when they are made diminutive the alif remains. You say for the diminutive of "إحدى" "أُحَيْدى", of "أحَد" "أُحَيْد", of "أَبانا" "أُبَيُّنا", and likewise "أُبَيّانِ" and "أُبَيُّونَ". Likewise [the alif in His words] ﴿مِنَ ٱلْمُهَاجِرِينَ وَٱلأَنْصَارِ﴾ and ﴿أُخْرِجْنَا مِن دِيَارِنَا وَأَبْنَآئِنَا﴾, because you say for "الأنصار" "أُنَيْصار", and for "الأنباءِ" "أُبَيْناء" and "أُبَيْنُون". [Translator's note: the source writes "الأنباء" here where the verse has "أبنائنا"; translated as written.]
Alifs at the start of a verb or a maṣdar where the "يَفْعل" form of that verb has a ḍamma on its yāʾ are disjunctive; at the beginning they stay as they are in connection, as in His words ﴿بِمَآ أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْكَ﴾, because you say "يُنْزَل" and the yāʾ has ḍamma. And ﴿رَبَّنَآ آتِنَا﴾ is disjunctive because the yāʾ has ḍamma, since you say "يُؤْتِى". He said ﴿وَبِٱلْوَالِدَيْنِ إِحْسَاناً﴾ and ﴿وَإِيتَآءِ ذِي ٱلْقُرْبَىٰ﴾, because you say "يُؤتِي" and "يُحْسِن". And His words ﴿وَقَالَ ٱلْمَلِكُ ٱئْتُونِي بِهِ أَسْتَخْلِصْهُ لِنَفْسِي﴾ and ﴿وَقَالَ فِرْعَوْنُ ٱئْتُونِي بِكُلِّ سَاحِرٍ عَلِيمٍ﴾: these are connecting, because you say "يَأتي" and the yāʾ has fatḥa. The hamza in His words ﴿وَقَالَ ٱلْمَلِكُ ٱئْتُونِي بِهِ﴾ is a hamza that belongs to the root, in the position of the fāʾ (first radical) of the verb; do you not see that it remains in "أتيت" and in "أتى" and does not drop? We will explain hamza to you in its place, God willing. His words ﴿آتِنَا﴾ may be from "آتى" and "آتاه الله", as you say "ذهب" (he went) and "أذهبه الله" (Allah made him go), and it may be in the sense of "أَعطنا" (give us). He said ﴿فَآتِهِمْ عَذَاباً﴾ on the pattern "فَعَل" and "أَفْعَلَهُ غيرُه" (someone else made him do it).
As for His words ﴿الرَّحْمٰنِ الرَّحِيـمِ ٱلْحَمْدُ﴾, these nouns that have alif and lām at their beginnings were connected, so that the alif disappeared in pronunciation. That is because in every noun beginning with an added alif and lām, the alif goes when it is joined to speech before it. When you begin with it, it always has fatḥa, to distinguish it from the alif that is added without the lām, and because this alif and lām are together a single particle, like "قد" and "بل". Their addedness is recognised by your attempting to put another alif and lām onto them: if you cannot do so, you know they are added. Do you not see that with your saying "الحمدُ للّهِ", and your saying "العالمين", and your saying "التي", "الذي" and "الله", you cannot put another alif and lām onto them? This shows that they are added; so whenever they are joined to what precedes them, the alif goes — except when the interrogative alif is joined to it, in which case it is left lightened [Translator's note: i.e. pronounced with madd rather than dropped], and [and] none of the Arabs lighten the hamza in it except a few people [Translator's note: the sentence is garbled in the source; translated as written], as in His words ﴿ءَآللَّهُ أَذِنَ لَكُمْ﴾, His words ﴿ءَآللَّهُ خَيْرٌ أَمَّا يُشْرِكُونَ﴾ and His words ﴿آلآنَ وَقَدْ عَصَيْتَ قَبْلُ﴾. It was lengthened in the interrogative only to distinguish the question from the statement. Do you not see that if, while asking, you said "الرجل قال كذا وكذا" (the man said such-and-such?) without lengthening it, it would become like your saying "الرجل قال كذا وكذا" when you make a statement?
Not all connecting alifs are like this. He said ﴿أَصْطَفَى ٱلْبَنَاتِ عَلَىٰ ٱلْبَنِينَ﴾, and He said ﴿أَفْتَرَىٰ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ كَذِباً أَم بِهِ جِنَّةٌ﴾. These alifs have fatḥa and are disjunctive, because they are the interrogative alif, and the connecting alif that was in "اصطفى" [and "افترى"] has gone, since the ṣād [and the fāʾ] were joined to this interrogative alif before them. And whoever read this verse ﴿كُنَّا نَعُدُّهُمْ مِّنَ ٱلأَشْرَارِ﴾ ﴿أَتَّخَذْنَاهُمْ﴾ with a disjunctive alif in "أَتخذناهم" made it the interrogative alif and dropped the connecting alif that came after it, because when it is joined to a letter before it, it goes. This word has also been read with a connecting alif; they took His words ﴿أَمْ زَاغَتْ عَنْهُمُ ٱلأَبْصَار﴾ as dependent on His words ﴿مَا لَنَا لاَ نَرَىٰ رِجَالاً كُنَّا نَعُدُّهُمْ مِّنَ ٱلأَشْرَارِ﴾ ﴿أَمْ زَاغَتْ عَنْهُمُ ٱلأَبْصَار﴾.
Any noun beginning with alif and lām onto which you can put another alif and lām has a disjunctive alif, which at the beginning stays as it is in connection, as in His words ﴿مَا لَكُمْ مِّنْ إِلَـٰهٍ غَيْرُهُ﴾, because if you said "الإِله", putting alif and lām onto it, that would be permissible. Likewise "أَلواح", "إلهام" and "إلقاء" are all disjunctive, because it is permissible to add another alif and lām. As for "إلى", it is disjunctive, and it is not permissible to put alif and lām onto it because it is not a noun; alif and lām are only put onto nouns. What shows you that the alif and lām in "إلى" are not added is that you find alif and lām added only in nouns, and they are not added in non-nouns such as "إلى" and "أَلاَّ". Moreover, the alif of "إلى" has kasra, whereas the alif of the added lām never has kasra.
As for His words ﴿ٱلْحَمْدُ للَّهِ﴾, it is nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject; lit. by inception, ibtidāʾ). That is because every noun you begin with, without making a verb after it act on it, is nominative (marfūʿ), and its khabar (predicate), if it is identical with it, is also nominative, as in His words ﴿مُّحَمَّدٌ رَّسُولُ ٱللَّهِ﴾ and the like. This general statement covers every mubtadaʾ in the Quran, so understand it. What makes the mubtadaʾ nominative is your beginning with it, and the inception (ibtidāʾ) is what made the khabar nominative in the view of some; [and] just as "أنَّ" puts the noun in the accusative and the khabar in the nominative, so the inception made the noun and the khabar nominative. Others said: "The mubtadaʾ made its khabar nominative." All of it is good, and the first is more consistent with analogy.
Some Arabs say ﴿ٱلْحَمْدَ للَّهِ﴾, making it accusative as a maṣdar. That is because for him the basic form of the speech is "حَمْداً لله", making it a substitute for pronouncing the verb, as if he put it in place of "أَحْمَدُ" (I praise) and made it accusative by "أَحْمَدُ", as though he said "أَحْمَدُ حَمْداً", and then put alif and lām onto it.
Some Arabs said ﴿ٱلْحَمْدِ للَّهِ﴾ with kasra. That is because he treated it like the nouns that are not fully declinable (ghayr mutamakkina). Nouns that are not fully declinable have their endings given one vowel whose cause does not go away, like "حَيْثُ", which some Arabs give ḍamma in every case, while some say "حَوْثُ" and "حَيْثَ", with ḍamma and fatḥa. And like "قَبْلُ" and "بَعْدُ", which were given ḍamma in every case. Allah the Blessed and Exalted said ﴿لِلَّهِ ٱلأَمْرُ مِن قَبْلُ وَمِن بَعْدُ﴾; they have ḍamma unless you make them muḍāf (put them in a genitive construct), and when you make them muḍāf you decline them. He said ﴿لاَ يَسْتَوِي مِنكُم مَّنْ أَنفَقَ مِن قَبْلِ ٱلْفَتْحِ وَقَاتَلَ﴾, ﴿كَٱلَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِكُمْ﴾ and ﴿وَٱلَّذِينَ جَآءُوا مِن بَعْدِهِمْ﴾, and He said ﴿مِّن قَبْلِ أَن نَّبْرَأَهَآ﴾; that is because His words ﴿أَن نَّبْرَأَهَآ﴾ are a noun to which ﴿قَبْل﴾ is put in construct. And He said ﴿مِن بَعْدِ أَن نَّزغَ ٱلشَّيْطَانُ﴾; that is because His words ﴿أَن نَّزغَ﴾ are a noun equivalent to "النَزْغ" (the stirring of discord), since the light "أنْ" and what it governs are equivalent to a noun, so "بَعْد" was put in construct with it. There is much of this in the Quran.
Among the nouns that are not fully declinable, Allah the Mighty and Majestic said ﴿إِنَّ هَؤُلآءِ ضَيْفِي﴾ and ﴿هَآأَنْتُمْ أُوْلاۤءِ تُحِبُّونَهُمْ﴾, with kasra in every case. In this dialect they likened "الحمد", which is a fully declinable noun, to these nouns that are not fully declinable, just as they said "يا زيدُ". In the Book of Allah: ﴿يٰهَامَانُ ٱبْنِ لِي صَرْحاً﴾; it is in the position of the accusative, because every vocative is in the position of the accusative, but it was likened to the not-fully-declinable nouns and left in one form. They say "ذهب أَمسِ بما فيه" (yesterday went with what was in it) and "لَقِيتهُ أمسِ يا فتى" (I met him yesterday, young man), giving it kasra in every position in some dialects. Some even said "لَقِيتهُ الأمسِّ الأحدث", also with genitive ending although it has alif and lām; that is hardly known.
We heard from Arabs one who says ﴿أَفَرَأَيْتُمُ ٱللاَّتِ وَٱلْعُزَّىٰ﴾, and says "هي اللاتِ قالت ذاك" (it is al-Lāt who said that), making it a tāʾ in the pause, and "هي اللاتِ فاعلم" (it is al-Lāt, know it), with genitive ending in the position of the nominative and accusative. Some said "من الآنَ إلى غد" (from now till tomorrow) with fatḥa, because it is a noun that is not fully declinable. As for his saying "اللاتِ فاعلم", this is like "أمسِ", and better, because the alif and lām in "اللات" do not drop even though they are added. As for what we heard in "اللات والعزى" when pausing on it, it is "اللاه", because it is a hāʾ that became a tāʾ in connected speech, and in that dialect it is like "كان من الأمر كيتِ وكيتِ" (such-and-such happened). Likewise "ههياتِ" [Translator's note: so in the source, for "هيهات"] in the dialect of those who give it kasra. However, "هيهات" may be a plural, so that its tāʾ is the feminine plural tāʾ, whereas that is not possible in "اللاتِ", because "اللات" and "كيت" cannot be plurals of the same kind: the tāʾ is not added in a plural except with the alif, and if you made the alif and tāʾ added, the noun would be left with one letter.
They claimed that some Arabs make the connecting alif disjunctive. Someone I trust told me that he heard someone say "يا إِبني" (O my son), making it disjunctive. Qays ibn al-Khaṭīm said [in the ṭawīl metre; this is the first evidentiary verse]:
‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌اذا جاوز الإِثنين سرٌّ فإنّه * بنشرٍ وتكثيرِ الوشاة قمين
(When a secret goes beyond two people, it is bound to be spread and multiplied by tale-bearers.)
And Jamīl said [in the ṭawīl metre; this is the second evidentiary verse]:
ألا لا أرى إِثنين أكرمَ شيمةً * على حدثانِ الدهر مني ومن جُمْلِ
(I see no two of nobler character, despite the blows of time, than me and Juml.)
And the rajaz poet said [this is the third evidentiary verse]:
يا نفسُ صبراً كلُّ حي لاق * وكلُّ إثنين إلى افتراق
(O soul, be patient: every living thing will meet [its end], and every two are bound to part.)
This is hardly known.
His words ﴿لِلَّهِ﴾ are genitive by the lām, just as His words
﴿رَبِّ ٱلْعَالَمِينَ الرَّحْمٰنِ الرَّحِيـمِ ﴾ are genitive, because they are an attribute of His words ﴿للَّهِ﴾. If it is said: "How can it be genitive when He said ﴿إِيّاك نَعْبُدُ [5]﴾." [Translator's note: the objection is left unanswered here in the source; the discussion appears to continue under verse 5.]
As for the fatḥa on the nūn of ﴿ٱلْعَالَمِينَ﴾, it is the nūn of the plural; likewise every [added] plural nūn formed on the pattern of the dual has fatḥa. It is the added nūn that does not change the noun from what it was, like the nūn of "مسلمين", "صالحين" and "مؤمنين". This nūn is added, because you say "مسلم" and "صالح" and the nūn goes; likewise "مؤمن", where the final nūn, the one with fatḥa, has gone; likewise "بنون". Do you not see that [you] have only added a wāw and nūn, or a yāʾ and nūn, to "مؤمن", and it remains as it was, its form unchanged, just as it was not changed in the dual when you said "مؤمنان" and "مؤمنين"? Except that you added an alif and nūn, or a yāʾ and nūn, for the dual. This nūn was given fatḥa only to distinguish it from the nūn of the dual, because the nūn of the dual always has kasra. He said ﴿قَالَ رَجُلاَنِ مِنَ ٱلَّذِينَ يَخَافُونَ أَنْعَمَ ٱللَّهُ﴾ and He said ﴿أَرْسَلْنَآ إِلَيْهِمُ ٱثْنَيْنِ فَكَذَّبُوهُمَا﴾, with the nūn having kasra.
The yāʾ was made for the accusative and genitive, as in "العالمينَ" and "المتقينَ", so their accusative and genitive are the same, just as the accusative and genitive of "الاثنينِ" were made the same; but the letter before the plural yāʾ has kasra and the letter before the dual yāʾ has fatḥa, to distinguish between dual and plural. The nominative was made with wāw, to be a sign of the nominative, and the nominative of the dual with alif.
This nūn falls away in the genitive construct just as the dual nūn falls away, as in your saying "بنوك" (your sons) and "ورأيت مسلميك" (I saw your Muslims). This nūn is not like the nūn of "الشياطين", "الدهاقين" and "المساكين", because in "الشياطين", "الدهاقين" and "المساكين" the nūn belongs to the root. Do you not see that you say [شيطان] and "شُييطين", "دِهقان" and "دُهَيْقين", "مِسْكين" and "مُسَيْكين", and the nūn does not fall away?
As for "الذينَ", its nūn has fatḥa, because you say "الذي" and the nūn falls away since it is added, and because you say in its nominative "اللذون"; for this is a noun that is not fully declinable, like "الذي". Do you not see that "الذي" remains in one state?
Except that some Arabs say "هم اللذون يقولون كذا وكذا" (they are the ones who say such-and-such). They gave it a sign of the nominative in the plural, because the plural must have a sign: wāw in the nominative, and yāʾ in the accusative and genitive, which is vowelless. So the vowelless yāʾ that was in "الذي" was dropped, because two vowelless letters do not come together, just as the yāʾ of "الذي" goes when you add the yāʾ of the accusative, and because they are both signs of declension. The yāʾ in the speech of those who say "هم الذين" is like a letter with fatḥa or kasra on which the noun is built, with no declension in it. But what shows you that it is the [form with] fatḥa or kasra in the nominative, accusative and genitive is the yāʾ for the accusative and genitive, because it is a sign of declension. [Translator's note: this last sentence is obscure in the source; translated as written.]
Some Arabs said "الشياطون", because they likened this yāʾ that was in "شياطين" — when a nūn came after it, it was in a plural, and a kasra was before it — to the yāʾ of declension in the plural. So when they came to the nominative they put in the wāw. This resembles "هذاجُحرُ ضبٍّ خَرِبٍ" (this is the hole of a lizard, ruined [with "ruined" given genitive by attraction]), so understand.

akhfash:4-4.t:
As for His words ﴿مَـٰلِكِ يَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ﴾, it is genitive (majrūr) because it is an attribute of "اللَّهِ", the Mighty and Majestic.
Some people read it ﴿مالكَ﴾, accusative as a supplication (ʿalā al-duʿāʾ, i.e. as a vocative), and that is permissible: both accusative and genitive are permissible in it. [And some people read it ﴿مَلْك﴾,] except that "المَلْك" (the king) is a noun not derived from a verb, as in your saying "مَلْك ومُلوك" (king, kings), whereas "المالك" (the owner) is the agent, as you say "مَلَك فهو مالِكٌ" (he owned, so he is an owner), like "قهر فهو قاهر" (he subdued, so he is a subduer).

akhfash:5-5.t:
﴿إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ﴾: [the second-person address is used] because, when He has said "الحمدُ لِمالِكِ يومِ الدين" (praise be to the Master of the Day of Judgement), He ought to say "إيّاهُ نعبد" (Him we worship); but this is according to the revelation. That is, Allah the Blessed and Exalted addressed the Prophet ﷺ and said: "Say, O Muhammad: 'الحمدُ لله'", and "Say: 'الحمدُ لمالكِ يومِ الدين'", and "Say, O Muhammad: ﴿إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ وَإِيَّاكَ نَسْتَعِينُ﴾".
As for His saying ﴿إيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ﴾ and not saying "أنت نعبد", [it is] because this is an accusative position. When, in an accusative position, the kāf or the hāʾ or similar pronouns used for the accusative cannot be used, "إِيّاك" or "إيَّاهُ" or the like, which stand in an accusative position, is used instead. He said ﴿وَإِنَّآ أَوْ إِيَّاكُمْ لَعَلَىٰ هُدًى﴾, because this is an accusative position; you say "إني أَو زيداً منطلق" (I or Zayd is leaving). And ﴿ضَلَّ مَنْ تَدْعُونَ إِلاَّ إِيَّاهُ﴾: this is in an accusative position, like your saying "ذهب القوم الاّ زيدا" (the people went, except Zayd). [And] ﴿إِيَّاكَ﴾ [in ﴿إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ﴾] is in an accusative position only because of ﴿نَعْبُدُ﴾; and likewise
﴿إِيَّاكَ نَسْتَعِينُ﴾ too. When the position is nominative, you put "أنت", "أنتما", "أنتم", "هو", "هي" and the like in it.

akhfash:6-6.t: As for His words ﴿ٱهْدِنَا ٱلصّرِاطَ ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمَ ﴾, He is saying: "عَرِّفْنا" (make us know). The people of the Hijaz say "هديتُه الطريقَ" (I guided him the way), meaning "I made him know it", and likewise "هديتُه البيتَ" (I guided him the house) in their dialect. Others attach "الى" (to) to it.

akhfash:7-7.t:
﴿صِرَاطَ ٱلَّذِينَ أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ is accusative as a badal (substitute). ﴿أَنْعَمْتَ﴾ has a disjunctive alif (alif qaṭʿ), because you say "يُنعِم" and the yāʾ has ḍamma, so understand. And His words
﴿غَيْرِ ٱلْمَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِم﴾: these are an attribute of ﴿ٱلَّذِينَ أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾, because "الصراط" is put in construct with them, so they are genitive by the construct, and "غير" was made to follow them as an attribute (naʿt) or a badal. "غَيْرٌ" and "مِثْلٌ" can be attributes of a definite noun with alif and lām, as in your saying "إني لأَمرّ بالرجلِ غيرِكَ وبالرجلِ مثلِكَ فما يشتمني" (I pass by the man other than you and by the man like you, and he does not insult me). "غيرٌ" and "مثلٌ" are properly only attributes of an indefinite noun, but they were needed in this position, so they were made to follow, as attributes, what has alif and lām. Taking "غير" as a badal is better than as an attribute, because "الذي" and "الذين" are never separated from the alif and lām, and they are more like a specific noun than "الرجل" and the like.
"الصراط" has two dialect forms, with sīn and with ṣād, but we choose the ṣād because it is written that way throughout the Quran.
The Arabs have said "هم فيها الجَمّاءَ الغفيرَ" (they are in it, all of them together) with the accusative, as if they had not put in the alif and lām, even though they made them explicit [Translator's note: the source has "اضهروهما", which may be a misprint for "أضمروهما" (implied them) or "أظهروهما" (made them explicit); rendered as the latter], just as they treated "مثلك" and "غيرك" like what has alif and lām even though they are not in the wording. This is only an attribute of a definite noun that comes in the sense of an indefinite. Do you not see that when you say "إنّي لأَمرُّ بالرجلِ مِثلك" you only mean "برجلٍ مثلِك" (by a man like you)? For you do not specify a particular man for him; and it is not permissible if you do specify that for him, unless you make it a badal; it cannot then be an attribute. Do you not see that "مررت بزيدٍ مثلِك" (I passed by Zayd, like you) is not permissible except as a badal? Similar is "إنّي لأَمُرُّ بالرجلِ من اهل البصرة" (I pass by the man from the people of Basra); if you said "إنّي لأَمُرُ بزيدٍ من أهل البصرة" it would not be permissible unless you put it in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial). Likewise ﴿غَيْرِ ٱلْمَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِم ﴾.
Some people read ﴿غَيْرِ ٱلْمَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِم﴾ [Translator's note: the source prints the genitive here, though the reading described — exception — would be accusative "غيرَ"], taking it as an exception that falls outside the first part of the speech. There is an explanation of that which we will mention, God willing: when, in the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, one makes an exception of something that is not from the first part of the speech, it is accusative; [and] * he says "ما فيها أحدٌ إلاّ حماراً" (there is no one in it except a donkey), while others say: "this is treated like what belongs to the first part", and make it nominative. So this one makes ﴿غَيْرِ ٱلْمَغْضُوبِ﴾ genitive in his dialect. [Translator's note: so in the source; the logic appears to be that in the non-Hijazi dialect the excepted word follows the declension of what precedes it, hence genitive.] If you wish, you can make "غير" accusative as a ḥāl, because it is indefinite and the first is definite; it was made genitive only by likening "الذي" to "الرجل". It is not good as an attribute, but [it is good] as a badal, as in ﴿بِٱلنَّاصِيَةِ﴾ ﴿نَاصِيَةٍ كَاذِبَةٍ﴾.
Some Arabs say
"هِيّاك" with hāʾ, making the alif of "إيّاك" a hāʾ, and saying "هِيّاك نعبد", just as you say "إيهِ" and "هِيهِ", and just as you say "هَرَقت" and "أَرَقْتُ" (I poured).
The people of the Hijaz treat "الصراط" as feminine, as they treat "الطريق" (road), "الزُقاق" (lane), "السبيل" (way), "السوق" (market) and "الكَلاّء" (harbour) as feminine. The Banū Tamīm treat all of these as masculine. The Banū Asad treat "الهُدى" (guidance) as feminine.

daas-irab:1-7.t:
﴿اسْمَ﴾: Regarding its derivation, the people of Basra held that it is derived from السمو, which is elevation, while the people of Kufa held that it is derived from السمة, which is a mark (sign). The alif was dropped in the basmala because of its frequent use. ﴿الرَّحْمنِ﴾: its pattern is فعلان and it carries the meaning of intensiveness (mubālagha); none is described by it except Allah the Exalted.
﴿الرَّحِيمِ﴾: its pattern is فعيل and it likewise carries the meaning of intensiveness.
﴿بِسْمِ﴾: a preposition and its genitive noun, both attached to (mutaʿalliq) an omitted verb, its implied form being "ابتدئ" (I begin), or to an omitted khabar (predicate), its implied form being "ابتدائي" (my beginning). ﴿اللَّهِ﴾: the Name of Majesty, muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct). ﴿الرَّحْمنِ﴾: a naʿt (adjective) of Allah. ﴿الرَّحِيمِ﴾: a second naʿt.
The clause of the basmala is initial (ibtidāʾiyya), a clause with no grammatical position. «[Note: Please refer to the introduction to learn the method of the book.]» ﴿الْحَمْدُ﴾: praise of something beautiful by speech. ﴿الرب﴾: the Owner and the Master; it may also mean the One who sets right and the Nurturer. ﴿الْعالَمِينَ﴾: plural of عالَم (with fatḥa on the lām), and it means all created beings. ﴿يَوْمِ الدِّينِ﴾: the Day of Recompense. ﴿الصِّراطَ﴾: the path. It is treated as masculine and feminine, the masculine being more common.
﴿الْحَمْدُ﴾: mubtadaʾ (subject), nominative (marfūʿ). ﴿لِلَّهِ﴾: the Name of Majesty is genitive (majrūr) by the lām, and both are attached to an omitted khabar, its implied form being "الحمد واجب" (praise is due).
﴿رَبِّ﴾: a naʿt of Allah, or a badal (substitute) from it. ﴿الْعالَمِينَ﴾: muḍāf ilayhi, genitive with the yāʾ because it is assimilated to the sound masculine plural.
﴿الرَّحْمنِ، الرَّحِيمِ﴾: two naʿts of Allah. ﴿مالِكِ﴾: a third naʿt. ﴿يَوْمِ﴾: muḍāf ilayhi. ﴿الدِّينِ﴾: a second muḍāf ilayhi.
﴿إِيَّاكَ﴾: a detached accusative pronoun, indeclinable (mabnī) on fatḥa, in the position of accusative as a fronted mafʿūl bihi (direct object). ﴿نَعْبُدُ﴾: an imperfect verb. ﴿وَإِيَّاكَ﴾: its i'rab has preceded. ﴿نَسْتَعِينُ﴾: an imperfect verb; its original form is نستعون — they found the kasra on the wāw heavy and transferred it to the ʿayn, and the wāw turned into yāʾ because of the kasra before it. ﴿اهْدِنَا﴾: an imperative verb intended as supplication, indeclinable on the dropping of the weak letter.
The fāʿil (agent) is a latent (mustatir) pronoun, its implied form being "أنت" (you), and نا is an attached pronoun in the position of accusative as mafʿūl bihi. ﴿الصِّراطَ﴾: a noun, accusative by removal of the preposition — or a second mafʿūl bihi. ﴿الْمُسْتَقِيمَ﴾: a naʿt of الصراط; its original form is مستقوم, like نستعين. ﴿صِراطَ﴾: a badal from الصراط — a badal of the whole from the whole. ﴿الَّذِينَ﴾: a relative noun, indeclinable on fatḥa, in the position of genitive by annexation (iḍāfa).
﴿أَنْعَمْتَ﴾: a past verb, indeclinable on sukūn, and the tāʾ is the tāʾ of the fāʿil; the clause أنعمت is the ṣila (relative clause) of the relative noun, with no grammatical position.
﴿عَلَيْهِمْ﴾: a preposition and its genitive noun, both attached to أنعمت. ﴿غَيْرِ﴾: a naʿt of الذين. ﴿الْمَغْضُوبِ﴾: muḍāf ilayhi. ﴿عَلَيْهِمْ﴾: both attached to المغضوب. ﴿وَلَا﴾: the wāw is a conjunction; لا is redundant (zāʾida), to reinforce the meaning of negation in غير. ﴿الضَّالِّينَ﴾: maʿṭūf (conjoined) to المغضوب عليهم, genitive with the yāʾ because it is a sound masculine plural. ﴿آمين﴾: a verbal noun of command (ism fiʿl amr) for supplication — it is not part of al-Fātiḥa — meaning "استجب" (answer [our prayer]); indeclinable on sukūn, and it was vowelled with fatḥa to suit the yāʾ preceded by a kasra.

farraa:1-1.t:
Al-Farrāʾ narrated to us; he said: The explanation of the difficult points of the i'rab of the Qur'an and of its meanings — Umm al-Kitāb (the Mother of the Book, i.e. al-Fātiḥa). He said:

The first of that is the agreement of the readers and of the copyists of the muṣḥafs on dropping the alif from ﴿بسم الله الرحمن الرّحيم﴾ [and at the openings of books, while they keep the alif in His words]: ﴿فَسَبِّحْ بِاسْمِ رَبِّكَ الْعَظِيمِ﴾. [They dropped it from ﴿بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم﴾ at the beginning of the surahs and of books only] because it occurs in a well-known place whose meaning the reader does not fail to know and which he does not need to read out; so dropping it was felt to be a lightening, since it is the way of the Arabs to be concise and to reduce what is lengthy once its meaning is known. It was kept in His words ﴿فَسَبِّحْ بِاسْمِ رَبِّكَ﴾ because it does not cling to this noun there, nor is it frequent with it as it is frequent with Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He. Do you not see that you say «بسم الله» at the start of every action you undertake: eating, drinking or slaughtering? So dropping it came easily to them because they knew it well.

I have seen some scribes whose familiarity with this place led them to drop both the alif and the sīn from «اسم», because they knew it and knew that the reader would not need to be told it. So never drop the alif of «اسم» when you annex it to something other than Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He, and never drop it with any of the ṣifāt [Translator's note: al-Farrāʾ's Kufan term for the prepositions] other than the bāʾ, even if that preposition is a single letter, such as the lām and the kāf. So you say: «لاسم الله حلاوة في القلوب» (the name of Allah has a sweetness in hearts) and «ليس اسم كاسم الله» (no name is like the name of Allah), keeping the alif after the lām and after the kāf, because they were not used as the bāʾ is used with the name of Allah. Among the things that became frequent in the speech of the Arabs, so that they dropped even more than this from it, is their saying «أيش عندك» (what do you have?): they dropped the inflection of «أي» and one of its two yāʾs, the hamza was dropped from «شيء», and the shīn was given a kasra though it had a fatḥa — and this is found in a great deal of speech that I cannot count.

If someone says: "We dropped the alif from «بسم الله» only because one cannot pause on the bāʾ, so it is permissible to begin the noun directly after it," he is told: The Arabs wrote in the muṣḥafs وَاضْرِبْ لَهُمْ مَثَلًا with the alif, though one cannot pause on the wāw — and so in many similar cases. This invalidates what he claimed.

farraa:2-2.t:
His words, Exalted is He: ﴿ٱلْحَمْدُ للَّهِ﴾. The readers agreed on the nominative (rafʿ) of «الحمد». As for the Bedouins, some of them say "الحمدَ لِلّه", some say "الحمدِ لِلّه", and some say "الحمدُ لُلّهِ", giving ḍamma to both the dāl and the lām.

As for the one who puts it in the accusative (naṣb), he says: "الحمد" is not a noun proper; it is only a maṣdar (verbal noun). Whoever says it could equally say: أحمد اللّه (I praise Allah). Whenever a verb (faʿala or yafʿalu) can stand in the place of the maṣdar, the accusative is permissible in it. An example is the word of Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He: ﴿فَإِذَا لَقِيتُمُ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ فَضَرْبَ ٱلرِّقَابِ﴾: in its place, in ordinary speech of the same kind, one could say: فاضربوا الرقاب (so strike the necks). Another is His word: ﴿مَعَاذَ ٱللَّهِ أَن نَّأْخُذَ إِلاَّ مَن وَجَدْنَا مَتَاعَنَا عِندَهُ﴾: in ordinary speech of the same kind you could say: نعوذ باللّه (we seek refuge in Allah). Likewise the Arabs' saying: سَقْيناً لكَ، ورَعْياً لك [Translator's note: «سَقْيناً» as printed; the well-known form is «سَقْياً»] (watering to you, and care to you), in whose place one may say: سقاك الله ورعاك الله (may Allah water you and care for you).

As for the one who gives kasra to the dāl of "الحمدِ", he says: This is a phrase that became so frequent on the tongues of the Arabs that it became like a single noun; and they found it heavy that a ḍamma followed by a kasra, or a kasra followed by a ḍamma, should come together within one noun of their speech, while they found that two kasras can come together in a single noun, as in إِبِل (camels). So they gave the dāl a kasra so that it would follow a pattern of their nouns.

As for those who give ḍamma to the lām, they intended the more common pattern of Arab nouns in which two ḍammas come together, such as الحُلُم (dream) and العُقُب (outcome).

Do not find it strange that two words should be treated as one when they are much used together. An example is the Arabs' saying "بِأَبَا" (by my father!), which is really "بِأَبِى": the yāʾ belongs to the speaker, not to «الأب»; but when the two were much used together they imagined them to be a single word and turned the yāʾ into an alif so that it would follow the pattern of حُبْلَى and سَكْرَى and similar words in the speech of the Arabs. Abū Tharwān recited to me:
قال الجوارِى ما ذَهَبْتَ مَذْهَبَا * وعِبْنَنِى ولم أكنْ مُعَيِّبَا
هل أنتَ إلا ذاهبٌ لِتلْعَبَا * أرَيْتَ إنْ أعطِيتَ نَهْداً كَعْثَبَا
أذاك أم نُعطيكَ هَيْدًا هَيْدَبَا * أَبْرَدَ فى الظَّلماء من مَسِّ الصَّبَا
فقلتُ: لا، بل ذا كما يا بِيَبَا * أجدرُ ألاّ تَفْضَحَا وتَحْرَبَا
(The girls said: "You have not gone any proper way," and they found fault with me though I was not one to be faulted: "Are you anything but one going off to play? Tell us: if you were given a full, plump one [Translator's note: a young woman], would you prefer that, or shall we give you a feeble, flabby old man, colder in the dark than the touch of the east wind?" I said: "No — rather that one, O my father [Translator's note: بِيَبَا], is more fitting, so that you two are not disgraced and despoiled.")
"هل أنتَ إلاّ ذاهبٌ لتلْعَبَا": he took "هل" in the sense of "ما" (not).

(عَلَيْهُم) and (عَلَيْهِم): these are two dialects, and each dialect has its rationale in Arabic. [Translator's note: the text passes here without transition from ﴿ٱلْحَمْدُ للَّهِ﴾ to «عليهم» of verse 7; it is translated as it stands.]

As for the one who gives ḍamma to the hāʾ, he says: its origin is ḍamma in its accusative, its genitive and its nominative. The nominative is as in their saying: "هُم قالوا ذاك" (they said that), at the beginning of a sentence — do you not see that it has ḍamma and may take neither fatḥa nor kasra? And the accusative is as in your saying "ضَرَبَهُم" (he struck them): it has ḍamma and may take neither fatḥa nor kasra. So in "عليهمُ" it was left in its original form.

As for the one who says "عليهِم", he found the ḍamma on the hāʾ heavy when a quiescent yāʾ precedes it, so he said "عليهِم", because of how often the pronoun (al-maknī) recurs in speech. They do the same with it when it is attached to a letter with kasra, as in "بِهِم" and "بِهُم": both ways are permissible in it, with a kasra and with a quiescent yāʾ.

It makes no difference whether the letter before the yāʾ has fatḥa or kasra; but when the letter before the yāʾ has fatḥa and it thus becomes an alif in pronunciation, only ḍamma is permissible in "هم", as in His word, Blessed and Exalted is He: ﴿وَرُدُّوۤاْ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ مَوْلاَهُمُ ٱلْحَقِِّ﴾ — one may not say "مَوْلاهِم الحقِّ" — and His word ﴿فَبِهُدَاهُمُ ٱقْتَدِهْ﴾ — one may not say "فبِهُداهِم اقْتَدهْ". Similar to this, among the things in which they used both ways when a quiescent yāʾ or a kasra precedes, is His word ﴿وَإِنَّهُ فِيۤ أُمِّ ٱلْكِتَابِ﴾ and ﴿حَتَّىٰ يَبْعَثَ فِيۤ أُمِّهَا رَسُولاً﴾: it is permissible to give ḍamma to the alif [Translator's note: i.e. the hamza] of "أمّ" and "أمها", and to give it kasra, in both words, because of the yāʾ. The kasra case is like His word, Blessed and Exalted is He: ﴿فَلأُمِّهِ ٱلسُّدُسُ﴾, and the wording of the one who narrated from the Prophet ﷺ: "أُوصى امرأً بِأمّه" (I enjoin a man [Translator's note: to be good] to his mother). Whoever uses ḍamma says: ḍamma is the original in الأمّ and الأمّهات; whoever uses kasra says: it is very frequent in speech, so a ḍamma preceded by a quiescent yāʾ or a kasra was felt heavy. Kasra on the alif of "أمّ" is permissible only when a kasra or a yāʾ precedes it. When the letter before it has fatḥa, as when you say: فلان عند أمّه (so-and-so is with his mother), you may not say: عند إِمّه. Likewise, when the letter before it has ḍamma, kasra is not permissible: you say اتّبعتُ أمّه (I followed his mother), and kasra is not permissible.

Likewise, when the letter before it is quiescent (majzūm), only ḍamma is possible on the alif of الأمّ, as when you say: من أُمّه and عن أُمّه. Do you not see that you say عنهُم, مِنهُم (and اضربهُم), and you do not say عنهِم, مِنهِم or اضِربهِم? So every place in which kasra of the hāʾ is good, as in their saying فيهم and the like, also allows kasra of the alif of "أمّ", and that is its analogy. You may not say: كتب إلى إِمّه (he wrote to his mother) nor على إِمّه, because what precedes it is an alif in pronunciation, though in writing it is a yāʾ: "إلى" and "على". Likewise: قد طالت يدا أُمه بالخير (his mother's hands have been generous with good); you may not say يدا إِمّه. But if you say: جلس بين يَدىْ أَمِّه (he sat before his mother), kasra and ḍamma are both permissible, because what precedes it is a yāʾ. Similarly, you say هم ضاربو أُمّهاتهم (they are beating their mothers) with ḍamma on the alif and nothing else, while you say ما هم بضاربى أُمّهاتهم and إِمّهاتهم (they are not beating their mothers), both ways being permissible because of the yāʾ. It makes no difference whether what precedes the alif of "أمّ" is joined to it or separate from it: both ways are permissible; you say هذهِ أمّ زيد and إِمُّ زيد (this is Zayd's mother). When you begin with it, it can only have ḍamma, just as "هُم" can only have ḍamma at the beginning. As for "هم", it takes kasra only with a letter attached to it that is not separated from it, as in "بِهِم".

farraa:7-7.t:
His words, Exalted is He: ﴿غَيْرِ ٱلْمَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِم﴾, with "غيرِ" in the genitive, because it is a naʿt (adjective) of «الذين», not of the hāʾ and mīm of "عليهم". "غير" may be an adjective of a definite noun here only because it has been annexed to a noun bearing alif and lām that is not aimed at a specific individual, and the first [Translator's note: i.e. «الذين»] is not aimed at a specific individual either. In speech it is like your saying: لا أمرّ إلا بالصادق غيرِ الكاذب (I pass by none but the truthful one, not the liar), as if you meant: by whoever is truthful and does not lie. You may not say: مررت بعبد الله غيرِ الظريفِ (I passed by ʿAbdallāh, not the witty one) except as repetition (takrīr, i.e. badal (substitute)), because ʿAbdallāh is specified (muwaqqat), while "غير" behaves like an unspecified indefinite and can only be an adjective of an unspecified definite. The accusative is permissible in "غير", making it a qaṭʿ [Translator's note: al-Farrāʾ's Kufan term, corresponding to ḥāl (circumstantial)] from "عليهم". It is also permissible to treat «الذين» before it as specified, and to put "غيرِ" in the genitive by repetition: "صراط غيرِ المغضوب عليهم" (the path of those not incurring wrath).

As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿وَلاَ ٱلضَّآلِّينَ﴾, the meaning of "غير" is the meaning of "لا" (not), and that is why "ولا" was brought back after it. It is as when you say: فلان غير محسن ولا مُجْمِل (so-and-so is not a doer of good, nor a doer of kindness). But when "غير" means "سوى" (other than), "لا" may not be repeated after it; do you not see that one may not say: عندى سوى عبد الله ولا زيد?

Someone who does not know Arabic has said: the meaning of "غير" in al-Ḥamd [Translator's note: i.e. al-Fātiḥa] is the meaning of "سوى", and "لا" is a ṣila (redundant particle) in the speech; and he adduced as proof the poet's words:
* في بئرِ لاحُورٍ سَرَى وما شَعَرْ *
(He travelled by night into a well of perdition [Translator's note: lit. "of no return"] and was unaware.)
This is [not] permissible, because the meaning here falls on something whose effect is not apparent, so it is pure negation. "لا" may be made a ṣila only when it is joined to a negation preceding it, as in the verse:
ما كان يرضى رسولُ اللهِ دينَهم * والطيِّبان أبو بكر ولا عمرُ
(The Messenger of Allah was not pleased with their religion, nor were the two good ones, Abū Bakr and ʿUmar.)
Here he made "لا" a ṣila because of the negation at the beginning of the speech. This explanation is clearer: in بئر لا حور he meant the genuine negating "لا", for he meant: in a well of water that brings back nothing [Translator's note: lit. "does not return anything"]; as if you said: he headed towards no right guidance and did not know it. The Arabs say: طحنت الطاحنةُ فما أحارت شيئا (the mill ground but produced nothing), i.e. no trace of its work appeared.

muyesser-irab:1-1.t:
﴿بسم﴾: a preposition and its genitive noun, attached to (mutaʿalliq) an omitted [verb], its implied form being "I begin" (أبتدئ), so the preposition and its genitive noun are in the position of an accusative (manṣūb) fronted mafʿūl bihi (direct object); or [its implied form being] "my beginning" (ابتدائي), so the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to an omitted khabar (predicate) of an omitted mubtadaʾ (subject).
﴿الله﴾: the Name of Majesty, muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct).
﴿الرحمن الرحيم﴾: two naʿts (adjectives) of Allah the Exalted; the clause of the basmala is initial (ibtidāʾiyya), a clause with no grammatical position.

muyesser-irab:2-2.t:
﴿الحمد﴾: mubtadaʾ (subject).
﴿لله﴾: a preposition and its genitive noun, attached to (mutaʿalliq) an omitted khabar (predicate).
﴿رب﴾: a naʿt (adjective) of «لله», or a badal (substitute) from it.
﴿العالمين﴾: muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct), genitive (majrūr), the sign of its genitive being the yāʾ in place of the kasra, because it is treated like the sound masculine plural.

muyesser-irab:3-3.t: ﴿الرحمن الرحيم﴾: two naʿts (adjectives) of Allah the Exalted as well.

muyesser-irab:4-4.t:
﴿مالك﴾: a fourth naʿt (adjective) of Allah.
﴿يوم الدين﴾: muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct).

muyesser-irab:5-5.t:
﴿إياك﴾: a detached pronoun in the position of an accusative (manṣūb), a fronted mafʿūl bihi (direct object), [fronted] for restriction (ikhtiṣāṣ).
﴿نعبد﴾: an imperfect verb, nominative (marfūʿ); its fāʿil (agent) is a pronoun necessarily latent (mustatir) in it, its implied form being "we" (نحن).
﴿وإياك نستعين﴾: conjoined to «إياك نعبد»; «نستعين»: an imperfect verb, nominative (marfūʿ); its fāʿil (agent) is a pronoun necessarily latent (mustatir) in it, its implied form being "we" (نحن).

muyesser-irab:6-6.t:
﴿اهدنا﴾: a verb of supplication, indeclinable (mabnī) on the omission of the weak [letter] (حذف العلة) [Translator's note: the source reads «حذف العلة», presumably for «حذف حرف العلة», "the omission of the weak letter"]; «نا» is an attached pronoun in the position of an accusative (manṣūb), mafʿūl bihi (direct object); its fāʿil (agent) is a pronoun necessarily latent (mustatir) in it, its implied form being "you" (أنت).
﴿الصراط﴾: a second mafʿūl bihi (direct object), or accusative by removal of the preposition (manṣūb bi-nazʿ al-khāfiḍ), because «هدى» is transitive only to one object, and is made transitive to the second by lām or by «إلى».
﴿المستقيم﴾: a naʿt (adjective) of «الصراط».

muyesser-irab:7-7.t:
﴿صراط﴾: a badal (substitute) of full correspondence (badal muṭābiq) from «الصراط».
﴿الذين﴾: a relative noun, muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct), in the position of a genitive (majrūr).
﴿أنعمت﴾: a past verb, indeclinable (mabnī) on sukūn because of its attachment to a vowelled nominative pronoun; the tāʾ is an attached pronoun in the position of a nominative (marfūʿ), fāʿil (agent); the clause «أنعمت» is a clause with no grammatical position, because it is the ṣila (relative clause) of the relative noun.
﴿عليهم﴾: a preposition and its genitive noun, attached to (mutaʿalliq) «أنعمت».
﴿غير﴾: a badal (substitute) from the pronoun in «عليهم», or from «الذين», or a naʿt (adjective) of «الذين».
﴿المغضوب﴾: muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct).
﴿عليهم﴾: a preposition and its genitive noun in the position of a nominative (marfūʿ), nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent) of «المغضوب», because it is a passive participle.
﴿ولا﴾: the wāw is a conjunction, and «لا» is a connective (ṣila) to emphasise the meaning of negation, namely the meaning of negation contained in «غير».
﴿الضالين﴾: conjoined (maʿṭūf) to «المغضوب عليهم», genitive (majrūr), the sign of its genitive being the yāʾ, because it is a sound masculine plural.

nahhas-irab:1-1.t:
(اسم) is in the genitive (makhfūḍ) through the redundant (zāʾida) bāʾ. Abū Isḥāq [al-Zajjāj] said: The bāʾ was given kasra to distinguish between what makes a noun genitive while being only a particle and nothing else, and what makes a noun genitive while it may sometimes be a noun, such as the kāf. It may be asked: why did the bāʾ come to make nouns genitive? The answer to this, and for all the genitive-governing particles, is that these particles have no meaning except in nouns, and they do not resemble verbs so as to govern as verbs govern; so they were given what occurs only in nouns, namely the genitive (khafḍ) — the early Basrans call it jarr. The position of the bāʾ and what follows it is, according to al-Farrāʾ, accusative, in the sense of "I began with «بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم»" or "I begin with «بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم»"; according to the Basrans it is nominative, in the sense of "my beginning is with the name of Allah". ʿAlī ibn Ḥamza al-Kisāʾī said:
The bāʾ has no grammatical position, and the "passing" falls upon something unspecified when you say: مررت بزيد ("I passed by Zayd").
The alif in «اسم» is a connecting alif (alif waṣl), because you say سُمَيّ (in the diminutive); for this reason it is dropped in pronunciation. As for its being dropped in writing, there are four views: al-Farrāʾ said it is because of frequent use; it is also reported [that it was dropped] because the bāʾ is never written separately; al-Akhfash Saʿīd said it was dropped because it is not part of the pronunciation; and the fourth view is that the original form is سِم and سُم. Abū Zayd recited: [al-Rajaz metre]
1-
بسم الذي في كلّ سورة سمه
(In the name of the One whose name is in every sura.)
— also with ḍamma, so that the original would be سما; then you brought the bāʾ and it became بسم, then the kasra was dropped and it became بسم. On this view there was never an alif in it at all. [Translator's note: the text as printed reads «ثم حذفت الكسرة فصار بسم» ("then the kasra was dropped and it became بسم"); the vowelling needed to follow the argument (presumably بِسِم → بِسْم) has been lost in the source.] The original pattern of اسم is fiʿl; it can only be that, for a reason that requires it. Its plural is أسماء, and the plural of أسماء is أسامي. You made اسم muḍāf (in a genitive construct) to Allah, Mighty and Majestic; the alif in "Allah" is a connecting alif according to those who say the original is لاه. Some of the Arabs make it a disjunctive alif (alif qaṭʿ) and say بسم الله [pronouncing the hamza], because it always accompanies the word, like a disjunctive alif.
«الرَّحْمنِ» is a naʿt (adjective) of Allah the Exalted. It is not put in the dual or plural, because it is used only of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The lām is assimilated into the rāʾ because of their closeness and because the lām of definiteness is so frequent.
«الرَّحِيمِ» is also a naʿt; its plural is رحماء. This [form] is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, Banū Asad, Qays and Rabīʿa; Banū Tamīm say رِحيم, رِغيف, بِعير [with kasra on the first letter]. [Translator's note: the printed text shows these words without vowelling; the Tamīmī kasra on the first letter is the well-known feature intended.] In pausing you may give the kasra a trace (ishmām) or make it quiescent; quiescence is better with what has kasra, and ishmām is more common with what has ḍamma.
The accusative is permissible in «الرَّحْمنِ الرَّحِيمِ» as praise (madḥ), and the nominative by implying a mubtadaʾ (subject); it is also permissible to make the first genitive and the second nominative, or to make one of them nominative and the other accusative.

nahhas-irab:2-2.t:
«الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ»: [الحمد] is nominative by being the mubtadaʾ (subject) according to the view of the Basrans. Al-Kisāʾī said: «الحمد» is nominative through the pronoun that is in the "ṣifa", the ṣifa being the lām — he treated the lām like a verb. Al-Farrāʾ said:
«الحمد» is nominative through the "maḥall", which is the lām — he treated the lām like a noun, because it cannot stand by itself. Al-Kisāʾī calls the genitive-governing particles ṣifāt ("qualifiers"), al-Farrāʾ calls them maḥāll ("places"), and the Basrans call them ẓurūf ("adverbials/containers"). Ibn ʿUyayna and Ruʾba ibn al-ʿAjjāj read «الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ» as a maṣdar (verbal noun) [i.e. in the accusative, الحمدَ لله], and this is the dialect of Qays and al-Ḥārith ibn Sāma. [Translator's note: the source prints the standard vowelling «الْحَمْدُ» here although it describes the accusative reading; likewise in the variant readings below, the printed Quranic text does not show the variant vowels being described.] The nominative is better both in wording and in meaning. As for wording: because it is a definite noun about which you have predicated. As for meaning: if you use the nominative you are stating that your praise and the praise of others belongs to Allah, Mighty and Majestic; if you use the accusative, it does not go beyond your own praise. Al-Farrāʾ reported: «الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ» and «الحمد لله» [i.e. الحمدِ لِلّه and الحمدُ لُلّه].
Abū Jaʿfar said: I heard ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān [al-Akhfash the Younger] say: neither of these two is permissible according to the Basrans. Abū Jaʿfar said: These are two known dialects and two existing readings, and each has a rationale. Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAyyāsh related from Zurayq from al-Ḥasan that he read «الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ» [i.e. الحمدِ لِلّه], and Ibrāhīm ibn Abī ʿAbla read «الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ» [i.e. الحمدُ لُلّه]; this is the dialect of some of Banū Rabīʿa, and the kasra is the dialect of Tamīm. As for the dialect with kasra: this phrase is very frequent in people's speech, and ḍamma is heavy, especially when a kasra follows it; so they replaced the ḍamma with kasra and treated the two as a single thing — kasra with kasra is lighter, and likewise ḍamma with ḍamma; that is why «الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ» was said [in these two ways].
«لِلَّهِ» is genitive through the lām, which is zāʾida (redundant). [Translator's note: the source says «باللام الزائدة»; the lām here is not normally classed as redundant, but it is translated as written.] Sībawayh held that the original vowel of the lām is fatḥa; what shows you this is that when you use a pronoun you say الحمد لَهُ, returning it to its origin; it was given kasra only with an overt noun, to distinguish between the lām of the genitive and the lām of emphasis (tawkīd).
«رَبِّ» is genitive as a naʿt (adjective) of Allah. «الْعالَمِينَ» is genitive by the iḍāfa (genitive construct); the sign of the genitive is the yāʾ, because it is of the same kind as kasra. The nūn, according to Sībawayh, is as it were a compensation for the vowel and the tanwīn that were withheld; according to Abū al-ʿAbbās [al-Mubarrad] the nūn is a compensation for the tanwīn; and according to Abū Isḥāq [al-Zajjāj] a compensation for the vowel. It was given fatḥa to distinguish it from the nūn of the dual. Al-Kisāʾī said: «رَبِّ الْعالَمِينَ» is permissible [in the accusative, ربَّ العالمين], as you say:
الحمد لله ربًّا وإلهًا ("praise be to Allah as Lord and God"), i.e. as a ḥāl (circumstantial). Abū Ḥātim said: the accusative is in the sense of "I praise Allah, the Lord of the worlds". Abū Isḥāq said: the accusative is permissible as a vocative (nidāʾ) in construct. Abū al-Ḥasan ibn Kaysān said: the accusative as a vocative in construct is far-fetched, because it would make it two separate utterances; rather it is accusative as praise (madḥ). The nominative is also permissible, i.e. "He is the Lord of the worlds". Abū Jaʿfar said: We mentioned in the earlier book that, for intensiveness, one says ربّاه, ربّه and ربّته. Its explanation is that the original is ربّبه, then a yāʾ is substituted for the bāʾ, as one says:
قصّيت أظفاري and تقصّيت [from قصّصت, "I clipped my nails"], then a tāʾ is substituted for the yāʾ, just as it is substituted for the wāw in تالله.

nahhas-irab:3-4.t:
«الرَّحْمنِ الرَّحِيمِ» is permissible [in the accusative] as praise (madḥ); it is permissible to make both nominative by implying a mubtadaʾ (subject); it is permissible to make one of them nominative and the other accusative; and it is permissible to make the first genitive and the second nominative or accusative.
Muḥammad ibn al-Samayfaʿ al-Yamānī read «مالك يوم الدّين» with مالك in the accusative. There are four dialectal forms of it: مالِك, مَلِك, مَلْك and مَلِيك, as Labīd said: [al-Kāmil metre] 2-
فاقنع بما قسم المليك فإنّما ... قسم المعايش بيننا علّامها
(Be content with what the Sovereign has apportioned, for the One who apportioned livelihoods among us is the One who knows them best.)
In terms of Arabic [grammar] there are twenty-five ways [of reading] it: one says «ملك يوم الدين» as a naʿt (adjective); in the nominative by implying a mubtadaʾ; in the accusative as praise, as a vocative, as a ḥāl (circumstantial), and as a naʿt according to the reading of those who read «رَبِّ الْعالَمِينَ» [in the accusative]. These are six ways; «مالك» has the same, «مَلْك» has the same, and «مليك» has the same. That makes twenty-four. The twenty-fifth is reported from Abū Ḥaywa Shurayḥ ibn Yazīd, that he read «ملك يوم الدّين», and it is also reported from him that he read «ملك يوم الدين». [Translator's note: the vowelling that distinguishes these two reported readings is missing from the source; in other works Abū Ḥaywa is credited with the verbal reading مَلَكَ يومَ الدين.] Abū Jaʿfar said: the plural of مالك is مُلّاك and مُلَّك; the plural of مَلِك is أملاك and ملوك; and the plural of مَلْك is أَمْلُك and ملوك — this on the view of those who say «مَلْك» is a dialectal form and not a quiescent-ised form of مَلِك. The plural of مليك is مُلَكاء.
«يَوْمِ» is genitive by مالك being put in construct with it, and «الدِّينِ» is genitive by يوم being put in construct with it. The plural of يوم is أيّام; the original is أَيْوام: the wāw was assimilated into the yāʾ. No verb is used from it.
Sībawayh held that if a verb were used from it, one would say يُمْتُ. The plural of الدين is أديان and ديون.

nahhas-irab:5-5.t:
«إِيَّاكَ» is accusative because «نَعْبُدُ» falls upon it [as its object]. Al-Faḍl ibn ʿĪsā al-Raqāshī read «إِيَّاكَ» with fatḥa on the hamza [أَيّاك], and ʿAmr ibn Fāʾid read «إِيَّاكَ» without shadda [إِياك]. [Translator's note: the source prints the standard form in both cases; the variants are as described in the words.] The noun in إيّاك, according to al-Khalīl and Sībawayh, is إيّا, and the kāf is in the position of the genitive; according to the Kufans, إيّاك in its entirety is the noun. Al-Khalīl, may Allah have mercy on him, held that it is a pronoun noun. Abū al-ʿAbbās said: this is a mistake — a pronoun is not put in construct; rather it is a vague noun (mubham) like «كلّ», put in construct with what follows it.
«نَعْبُدُ» is an imperfect verb (fiʿl mustaqbal); it is nominative according to al-Khalīl and Sībawayh because of its resemblance to nouns. Al-Kisāʾī said: the imperfect verb is nominative through the added letters at its beginning. Al-Farrāʾ said: it is nominative through its being free from the jussive- and subjunctive-governing particles.
The [second] «إِيَّاكَ» is accusative through «نستعين» — a clause conjoined to a clause. Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb and al-Aʿmash read «نَسْتَعِينُ» with kasra on the nūn [نِستعين], and this is the dialect of Tamīm, Asad, Qays and Rabīʿa. They did this to show that it is from استعون يستعين. The original of «نستعين» is نستعوِن: the vowel of the wāw was transferred to the ʿayn, and when what precedes the wāw had kasra it became a yāʾ. The maṣdar (verbal noun) is استعانة, the original being استعوان: the vowel of the wāw was transferred to the ʿayn, and when what precedes the wāw had fatḥa it became an alif. Two quiescent letters cannot meet, so the second alif was dropped because it is the augment — and it is said [rather] the first, because the second carries a meaning — and the hāʾ [tāʾ marbūṭa] was made obligatory as a compensation.

nahhas-irab:6-6.t:
«إِنَّا هُدْنا» [Translator's note: so printed in the source; the word under discussion is clearly «اهْدِنَا» of verse 6, and the heading appears to be a transcription error.] — it is a supplication and a request; according to al-Farrāʾ it is in the position of the jussive (jazm), and according to the Basrans it is in a state of pause (waqf) [i.e. indeclinable], and for that reason the yāʾ was dropped. The alif is a connecting alif (alif waṣl), because the first letter of the imperfect has fatḥa; you gave it kasra because it is from يهدي. The nūn and alif are the first mafʿūl bihi (direct object), and «الصِّراطَ» is the second object. Its plural of paucity is أَصْرِطة and its plural of abundance is صُرُط. Al-Akhfash said: the people of the Hijaz treat الصراط as feminine. Ibn ʿAbbās read «السراط» with sīn, and some of Qays pronounce it between ṣād and zāy; it is not permissible to make it a [pure] zāy unless it is quiescent. Quṭrub said: if, after the sīn within the same word, there is a ṭāʾ, a qāf, a khāʾ or a ghayn, you may change it into a ṣād.
«الْمُسْتَقِيمَ» is a naʿt (adjective) of الصراط.

nahhas-irab:7-7.t:
«صِراطَ الَّذِينَ»: [صراط] is a badal (substitute). «الَّذِينَ» is in the position of the genitive by the iḍāfa (genitive construct); it is indeclinable (mabnī) so that a noun is not declined from its middle. «أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ» is part of the ṣila (relative clause), and the hāʾ and mīm refer back to الذين. In «عليهم» there are five dialectal forms, all of which have been read. Ibn Abī Isḥāq read «أنعمت عليهُمُو» with ḍamma on the hāʾ and the wāw retained; this is the original, that the wāw be retained just as the alif is retained in the dual. Al-Ḥasan read «أنعمت عليهِمِي» with kasra on the hāʾ and the yāʾ retained: he gave the hāʾ kasra because he disliked combining a yāʾ and a ḍamma, the hāʾ being no strong barrier, and he substituted yāʾ for the wāw because what preceded it had kasra. The people of Medina read «عَلَيْهِمْ» with kasra on the hāʾ and the mīm quiescent; this is the dialect of the people of Najd. Ḥamza and the people of Kufa read «عَلَيْهُمْ» with ḍamma on the hāʾ and the mīm quiescent; they dropped the wāw because of its heaviness, and because the meaning is not ambiguous since in the dual one says عليهما. The fifth form was read by al-Aʿraj: «عليهِمُو» with kasra on the hāʾ and [ḍamma before] the wāw. [Translator's note: the source says «بكسر الهاء والواو», literally "with kasra of the hāʾ and the wāw"; translated as written, with the intended form supplied in brackets.] Two anomalous forms are also reported: ḍamma on both the hāʾ and the mīm without wāw, and kasra on both without yāʾ. [Translator's note: the source reads «لغتنا», evidently for «لغتان», "two dialectal forms".] Muḥammad ibn Yazīd [al-Mubarrad] said: this is not permissible, because it is mustaqbal [Translator's note: so in the source; the word seems corrupt — perhaps «مستثقل», "felt to be heavy"]. If it is asked: why then is منهُ said, with ḍamma on the hāʾ? The answer is that the nūn in «منه» is quiescent. Abū al-ʿAbbās said: some people of Banū Bakr ibn Wāʾil say عليكِم, giving the kāf kasra just as they give the hāʾ kasra, because it is a voiceless (mahmūsa) letter like it, and it is a pronoun just as the hāʾ is a pronoun. This is a gross error, because it is not like it in faintness.
«غَيْرِ الْمَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمْ» is genitive as a badal (substitute) from الذين, or, if you wish, as a naʿt (adjective). Ibn Kaysān said: it may also be a badal from the hāʾ and mīm in عليهم. Al-Khalīl, may Allah have mercy on him, related from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kathīr «غَيْرَ الْمَغْضُوبِ» in the accusative. Al-Akhfash said: it is accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial), or, if you wish, as an exception (istithnāʾ). Abū al-ʿAbbās said: it is an exception not of the same kind as what precedes (istithnāʾ laysa min al-awwal). The Kufans said: it cannot be an exception, because «ولا» comes after it, and «لا» is not added in exception. Abū Jaʿfar said: this does not follow, because it carries the meaning of negation. He said «غير المغضوب عليهم» and did not say "المغضوبين" because there is no pronoun in it. Ibn Kaysān said: it is singular with a plural meaning, and so is every passive participle when it has no nominative pronoun [Translator's note: the source reads «إذا لم يكن فيه خفض مرفوع», literally "when it has no nominative genitive"; the wording seems disturbed and is rendered by sense], such as المنظور إليهم and المرغوب فيهم. «الْمَغْضُوبِ» [is genitive] by غير being put in construct with it, and «عَلَيْهِمْ» is in the position of the nominative because it is the noun whose agent is not named [i.e. the nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent)].
«وَلَا» is zāʾida (redundant) according to the Basrans and in the sense of غير according to the Kufans. «الضَّالِّينَ» is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to «المغضوب عليهم»; the Kufans call this nasq, and Sībawayh calls it ishrāk ("association"). The original of الضالّين is الضاللين; then the lām was assimilated into the lām, so two quiescent letters met, and this was allowed because the alif has prolongation and the second is assimilated. However, Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī used a hamza and read «وَلَا الضَّأْلِّينَ».

zajjaj:1-1.t:
بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ
Abū Isḥāq Ibrāhīm ibn al-Sarī al-Zajjāj said: This is an abridged book on the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of the Qur'an and its meanings; and we ask Allah for success in all matters.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ﴾: What brings in the bāʾ is the meaning of beginning, as though you said: "بَدَأْتُ بِاسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ" (I begin with the name of Allah, the All-Merciful, the Most Merciful), except that there was no need to mention "بَدَأْتُ", because the situation (al-ḥāl) shows that you are beginning. The alif dropped from "بِاسْمِ اللَّهِ" in pronunciation, the original being "بِاسْمِ اللَّهِ", because it is a connecting alif (alif waṣl), which was brought in to make it possible to pronounce the vowelless letter. The proof of this is that when you form the diminutive of اسم you say "سُمَيٌّ". The Arabs say: "هَذا اِسْمٌ", "هَذا اُسْمٌ" and "هَذا سِمٌ". The rajaz poet said:
بِاسْمِ الَّذِي في كُلِّ سُورَةٍ سِمُهُ
(In the name of the One whose name is in every sura.)
— and "سُمُهُ" as well; Abū Zayd al-Anṣārī and other grammarians transmitted this. So the alif dropped for the reason we mentioned. Likewise your saying "اِبْنٌ": the alif in it is a connecting alif; you say in its diminutive "بُنَيٌّ". The meaning of our word "اِسْمٌ" is that it is derived from "اَلسُّمُوُّ", and "اَلسُّمُوُّ" is elevation. Its origin is "سَمَوٌ", with wāw, on the pattern of "جَمَلٌ", and its plural is "أسْماءٌ", like "قِنْوٌ" / "أقْناءٌ" and "حَنْوٌ" / "أحْناءٌ". The name (ism) was made only as an exalting of the meaning by the name of Allah, because the meaning lies beneath the name.

Whoever says that اسم is taken from "وَسَمْتُ" (I marked) is mistaken, because we know of nothing that a connecting alif has entered and whose fāʾ — I mean the fāʾ of the verb (the first radical) — has been dropped, as in your saying "عِدَةٌ" and "زِنَةٌ", whose origin is "وَعْدَةٌ" and "وَزْنَةٌ". If "اِسْمٌ" were "وَسْمَةٌ", its diminutive, once the connecting alif is dropped from it, would be "وُسَيْمٌ", just as the diminutive of "عِدَّةٌ" and "صِلَةٌ" is "وُعَيْدَةٌ" and "وُصَيْلَةٌ". No one can show a connecting alif in any noun whose fāʾ has been dropped. The alif dropped in writing from "بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ" but did not drop in ﴿اقْرَأْ بِاسْمِ رَبِّكَ الَّذِي خَلَقَ﴾ [al-ʿAlaq: 1], because in it (the basmala) there combined — together with its dropping in pronunciation — frequency of use.

Sībawayh held that the meaning of the bāʾ is attachment (ilṣāq). You say: "كَتَبْتُ بِالقَلَمِ" (I wrote with the pen), the meaning being that the writing is attached to the pen. It is always vowelled with kasra, because it has no meaning other than the genitive (khafḍ), so its pronunciation had to be with kasra, to distinguish between what puts into the genitive while being a noun — like the kāf in your saying "كَزَيْدٍ" — and what puts into the genitive while being a particle — like "بِزَيْدٍ". For the basic vowel of the particles that are spoken and consist of a single letter is always fatḥa, unless some cause comes along that removes it, because a single letter has no share in inflection (iʿrāb); but it occurs at the beginning of speech, and one cannot begin with a vowelless letter, so fatḥa was chosen, because it is the lightest of the vowels. You say: "رَأيْتُ زَيْدًا وعَمْرًا", and the wāw has fatḥa; likewise "فَعَمْرًا": the fāʾ has fatḥa. The lām was given kasra in your saying "لِزَيْدٍ" only to distinguish between the lām of the oath and the lām of annexation (lām al-iḍāfa). Do you not see that if you said "إنَّ هَذا لِزَيْدٍ" (this belongs to Zayd), it would be known that it is his property, and if you said "إنَّ هَذا لَزَيْدٌ" (this is indeed Zayd), it would be known that the one pointed at is Zayd? That is why the lām was given kasra in your saying "لِزَيْدٍ". If you said "إنَّ هَذا المالَ لَكَ" and "إنَّ هَذا لَأنْتَ", you would give the lām fatḥa, because the ambiguity has gone.

What we have said about the lām is the doctrine of Sībawayh, Yūnus, al-Khalīl, Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ and all the grammarians whose knowledge is trusted. Likewise you say "أزَيْدٌ في الدّارِ؟" (Is Zayd in the house?), and the alif (hamza) has fatḥa. Among the initial particles consisting of a single letter there is no letter with kasra except the bāʾ and the lām of command alone, and they were given kasra only for the cause we mentioned; and likewise the lām of annexation, whose basic vowel is fatḥa. As for the lām of "كَيْ" in your saying "جِئْتُ لِتَقُومَ يا هَذا" (I came so that you would stand, O you), it is the lām of annexation that is in your saying "اَلْمالُ لِزَيْدٍ" (the property belongs to Zayd); "تَقُومَ" is put in the accusative only by an implied "أنْ", or by "كَيْ" which has the meaning of "أنْ"; so the meaning is: "جِئْتُ لِقِيامِكَ" (I came for your standing). What we have said on the derivation of "اِسْمٌ" is a view that we know no one explained before us.

As for your saying "لِيَضْرِبْ زَيْدٌ عَمْرًا" (let Zayd strike ʿAmr), the lām was given kasra only to differentiate it from the lām of emphasis (tawkīd); its resemblance to the lām of the genitive does not matter, because the lām of the genitive does not occur with verbs, whereas the lām of emphasis does occur with verbs. Do you not see that if you said "لَتَضْرِبْ" while commanding, it would resemble the lām of emphasis when you say "إنَّكَ لَتَضْرِبُ" (you indeed strike)? This is the sum of what there is concerning the particles that consist of a single letter. As for the name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, the alif in it is a connecting alif; and I dislike mentioning everything the grammarians have said about the name of Allah — I mean our saying "اللَّهِ" — out of reverence for Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ﴾ [al-Fātiḥa: 3]: these are attributes of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He. Their meaning, according to what Abū ʿUbayda mentioned, is: "the Possessor of mercy". It is not permissible to say "اَلرَّحْمَنُ" of anyone but Allah. That is only because the pattern "فَعْلانُ" is among the patterns of what is described intensively. Do you not see that when you say "غَضْبانُ", its meaning is "the one filled with anger"? So "رَحْمَنُ" is the One whose mercy encompasses everything; hence it is not permissible to call anyone other than Allah "رَحْمَنُ". These attributes were put in the genitive because they are praise of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, so their i'rab is the i'rab of His name. If you said — outside the Qur'an — "بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الكَرِيمَ" and "اَلْكَرِيمُ", and "اَلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبَّ العالَمِينَ" and "رَبُّ العالَمِينَ", that would be permissible. Whoever puts "رَبَّ العالَمِينَ" in the accusative does so only because it is praise of Allah: as though, when he said "اَلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ", it was inferred from this wording that he is mentioning Allah, so his saying "رَبَّ العالَمِينَ" is as though he said "أذْكُرُ رَبَّ العالَمِينَ" (I mention the Lord of the worlds). And when he says "رَبُّ العالَمِينَ", it is on the pattern of your saying "هو رَبُّ العالَمِينَ" (He is the Lord of the worlds). The poet said:
وَكُلُّ قَوْمٍ أطاعُوا أمْرَ مُرْشِدِهِمْ ∗∗∗ إلّا نُمَيْرًا أطاعَتْ أمْرَ غاوِيها
اَلظّاعِنِينَ ولَمّا يُظْعِنُوا أحَدًا ∗∗∗ والقائِلِينَ لِمَن دارٌ نُخَلِّيها
(Every tribe obeyed the command of its right guide, except Numayr, which obeyed the command of the one who led it astray — those who depart though they have made no one depart, and who say: "For whom is a home that we shall vacate?")
So "اَلظّاعِنِينَ" may be put in the accusative in two ways: as following "نُمَيْرًا", and as dispraise (dhamm), as though he said "أذْكُرُ الظّاعِنِينَ" (I mention those who depart). You may also put it in the nominative, meaning "هُمُ الظّاعِنُونَ" (they are those who depart). Likewise in "اَلْقائِلِينَ" you have the accusative and the nominative: you may put both in the nominative, you may put both in the accusative, you may put the first in the nominative and the second in the accusative, and you may put the first in the accusative and the second in the nominative. There is no disagreement among the grammarians about what we have described.

And from Sūrat "al-Ḥamd"
﷽
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿الحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ العالَمِينَ﴾: the meaning of "اَلْحَمْدُ" is thanks and praise of Allah the Exalted. ﴿الحَمْدُ﴾ is in the nominative by being the mubtadaʾ (subject; ibtidāʾ), and His saying ﴿لِلَّهِ﴾ is a predication about al-ḥamd. The preferred form in ordinary speech is the nominative. As for the Qur'an, ﴿الحَمْدُ﴾ is read in it only in the nominative, because the Sunna is followed in the Qur'an, and no attention is paid in it to anything other than the sound transmission which the readers renowned for precision and reliability have read; and the nominative is the reading. In ordinary speech it is permissible to say "اَلْحَمْدَ", meaning "أحْمَدُ اللَّهَ الحَمْدَ" (I praise Allah with praise), dispensing with mention of "أحْمَدُ" because the state of praise is the one creatures ought to be in; but the nominative is better and more eloquent in praising Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He. It has been transmitted from some people among the Arabs: "اَلْحَمْدَ لِلَّهِ" and "اَلْحَمْدِ لِلَّهِ"; this is the dialect of people who are paid no attention, and with whose transmission one does not occupy oneself. We have occupied ourselves with transmitting this form only to warn people against using it, or lest an ignorant person think that it is permissible in the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, or in speech. Nothing analogous to it has come in the speech of the Arabs, and there is no justification for it.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿رَبِّ العالَمِينَ﴾: we have already explained that in the Qur'an only ﴿رَبِّ العالَمِينَ﴾ ﴿الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ﴾ [al-Fātiḥa: 3] is permissible, even though the nominative and the accusative are permissible in ordinary speech; for the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, only the best and most eloquent wording is chosen.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿العالَمِينَ﴾: its meaning is everything that Allah created, as He said: "وَهو رَبُّ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ" (and He is the Lord of everything). It is the plural of "عالَمٌ"; you say "هَؤُلاءِ عالَمُونَ" and "رَأيْتُ عالَمِينَ". "عالَمٌ" has no singular from its own root-form, because "عالَمٌ" is a collective for different things; and if "عالَمٌ" is used for one of them, it becomes a plural for similar things. The nūn in "اَلْعالَمِينَ" was given fatḥa because it is the nūn of the plural. Sībawayh held that it was given fatḥa to distinguish it from the nūn of the dual: you say "هَذانِ عالَمانِ يا هَذا", giving the nūn of the dual kasra because of the meeting of two vowelless letters — and this is explained in its place, if Allah wills. Likewise the nūn of the plural was vowelled with fatḥa because of the meeting of two vowelless letters, and was not given kasra because kasra is heavy after wāw and yāʾ. Do you not see that you say "سَوْفَ أفْعَلُ", giving the fāʾ of "سَوْفَ" fatḥa because of the meeting of two vowelless letters, and not kasra because kasra is heavy after wāw? Likewise you say "أيْنَ زَيْدٌ؟", giving the nūn fatḥa because of the meeting of two vowelless letters after yāʾ.

zajjaj:2-2.t:
And from Sūrat "al-Ḥamd"
﷽
